profile.headline: A faecal-oral hepatitis that never becomes chronic, is entirely vaccine-preventable, and gets more dangerous the later in life it is acquired.
profile.syndrome: Abrupt fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort, then jaundice with dark urine and pale stools. Asymptomatic in most children under six, which is what sustains silent transmission. Prolonged cholestatic and relapsing courses occur; fulminant hepatic failure in well under 1%, concentrated in older adults and in those with chronic liver disease.
profile.transmission: Faecal-oral: person-to-person in households and childcare, and through contaminated water, shellfish, frozen berries and food handled by an infected person. Outbreaks occur among men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs and people experiencing homelessness, and the virus is shed at highest titre in the two weeks before jaundice.
profile.reservoir: Humans, essentially exclusively; non-human primates can be infected but maintain nothing.
profile.geography: Worldwide, with the epidemiology inverted by sanitation: where it is poor almost everyone is infected in early childhood and disease is rare, and where sanitation improves infection is deferred to adulthood and outbreaks become severe.
profile.diagnosis: Anti-HAV IgM, which is detectable from the onset of symptoms and persists for three to six months; HAV RNA in outbreak investigation and to link cases to a food source.
profile.management: Supportive. No specific antiviral exists and none is needed in most cases; transplantation for the rare fulminant presentation.
profile.prevention: Inactivated vaccine, highly effective and long-lasting, given pre-exposure to travellers and risk groups and as post-exposure prophylaxis within 14 days — which works because the incubation period is longer than the immune response takes. Immune globulin for infants under one, the immunocompromised and those with chronic liver disease. Safe water, sanitation and food hygiene.
evidence: Established by human volunteer studies in the 1940s-60s, virus identification in 1973 and randomised vaccine trials; the post-exposure window is supported by trial evidence of vaccine non-inferiority to immune globulin.
